from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Data is organized in a grid.", "We scan with a small window.", "The window looks at local neighborhoods."]
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisites: The Sliding Window Concept", lecture_lines)
        
        # Create 1D array
        array_size = 8
        cells = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.6, color=WHITE) for _ in range(array_size)])
        cells.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0)
        self.place_in_area(cells, 'C2', 'C5', scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Create sliding window
        window = Square(side_length=0.6, color=YELLOW)
        window.surrounding_rectangle = SurroundingRectangle(cells[0], color=YELLOW, buff=0)
        
        # Initial State
        self.play(FadeIn(cells))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#87CEEB")) # SkyBlue
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#90EE90")) # LightGreen
        
        window_rect = SurroundingRectangle(cells[0:2], color="#FF4500", buff=0)
        self.play(Create(window_rect))
        
        # Slide the window
        for i in range(array_size - 1):
            target_rect = SurroundingRectangle(cells[i:i+2], color="#FF4500", buff=0)
            self.play(Transform(window_rect, target_rect), run_time=0.5)
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFD700")) # Gold
        
        # Highlight local neighborhood
        self.play(window_rect.animate.set_stroke(width=6), run_time=1)
        self.wait(1)
        
        self.play(FadeOut(window_rect))
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Convolution blends two functions together.",
            "We flip, slide, multiply, and sum.",
            "The kernel slides over the input.",
            "Each overlap creates one output value.",
            "This forms a new feature map."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Defining Discrete Convolution", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # 1. Define formula (f * g)[n] = Σ f[k]g[n-k]
        formula = MathTex(r"(f * g)[n] = \sum_{k} f[k] \cdot g[n-k]", color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_in_area(formula, "A1", "B6")
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # 2. Show function f and kernel g as arrays.
        f_arr = Matrix([[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]])
        g_arr = Matrix([[0, 1, 0]])
        f_label = Text("f", font_size=20).next_to(f_arr, UP)
        g_label = Text("g", font_size=20).next_to(g_arr, UP)
        content = VGroup(f_label, f_arr, g_label, g_arr).arrange(DOWN)
        self.place_in_area(content, "C1", "E3")
        self.play(Create(f_arr), Write(f_label), Create(g_arr), Write(g_label))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # 3. Flip kernel g horizontally, show in #FFFF00.
        g_flipped = Matrix([[0, 1, 0]])
        g_flipped.set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.play(Transform(g_arr, g_flipped))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # 4. Slide kernel g over f, calculate sum-product.
        # Just a placeholder visual representation of the slide
        brace = Brace(f_arr, DOWN)
        text_slide = Text("Slide", font_size=18).next_to(brace, DOWN)
        self.play(Create(brace), Write(text_slide))
        self.play(g_arr.animate.shift(RIGHT * 0.5), run_time=1)
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#7FFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # 5. Display result array in #7FFF00.
        res_arr = Matrix([[0, 1, 2, 1, 0]])
        res_arr.set_color("#7FFF00")
        res_label = Text("Result", font_size=20).next_to(res_arr, UP)
        res_group = VGroup(res_label, res_arr)
        self.place_in_area(res_group, "E4", "F6")
        self.play(Write(res_label), Create(res_arr))
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#7FFF00")
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Kernels act as feature extractors.",
            "Values inside determine the transformation.",
            "Sharp gradients detect image edges.",
            "Balanced values smooth the output.",
            "Kernels help computers see structure."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The 'Effect' of the Kernel", lecture_lines)
        
        input_label = Text("Input", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        output_label = Text("Output", font_size=24, color=WHITE)

        input_rect = Rectangle(width=1.5, height=1.5, color=GREY).set_fill(GREY, opacity=0.5)
        kernel_rect = Rectangle(width=1, height=1, color="#FF00FF").set_fill("#FF00FF", opacity=0.5)
        output_rect = Rectangle(width=1.5, height=1.5, color=GREY).set_fill(GREY, opacity=0.5)

        self.place_at_grid(input_rect, 'B2')
        self.place_at_grid(input_label, 'A2')
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.play(FadeIn(input_rect), FadeIn(input_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.place_at_grid(kernel_rect, 'B4')

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application: Image Processing & AI", 
                          ["CNNs stack these convolution operations.", 
                           "They recognize complex, layered objects.", 
                           "Simple features become complex images."])
        
        # 1. Convolutional Neural Network layer diagram concept
        # Representing a small 3x3 kernel and output
        grid_square = Square(side_length=0.6, color=WHITE).set_fill(GREY, opacity=0.3)
        kernel = VGroup(*[grid_square.copy() for _ in range(9)]).arrange_in_grid(3, 3, buff=0.05)
        self.place_at_grid(kernel, 'B2', scale_factor=0.8)

        # Output activation map
        output_map = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.4, color=WHITE).set_fill(BLACK, opacity=0.8) for _ in range(16)]).arrange_in_grid(4, 4, buff=0.05)
        self.place_at_grid(output_map, 'E5', scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.add(kernel, output_map)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # CNNs stack these convolution operations.
        # Highlight kernel filter weights
        self.play(kernel.animate.set_color("#00CED1"), run_time=1.0)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#00CED1"), run_time=0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # They recognize complex, layered objects.
        # Highlight activation map
        self.play(output_map.animate.set_color("#FF8C00"), run_time=1.0)
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF8C00"), run_time=0.5)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Simple features become complex images.
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW), run_time=0.5)
        self.wait(1)

outline.topic: Understanding Discrete Convolutions: From Filters to Features
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate Computer Science or Engineering students

sections.title: Prerequisites: The Sliding Window Concept (0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the idea of a 'local neighborhood'. Before convolution, understand that data (like a 1D sequence or 2D image) is treated as a grid. We move a small 'window' across this grid to look at subsets of data sequentially.
sections.example: Imagine a detective using a magnifying glass to scan a long scroll of paper one section at a time.

sections.title: Defining Discrete Convolution (1:15)
sections.content: Define convolution as a mathematical operation between two functions (the input signal and a kernel/filter). Explain the process: 'Flip, Slide, Multiply, and Sum'. Use a visual graphic showing the Kernel overlapping the Signal, multiplying corresponding values, and producing a single output point.
sections.example: Visualizing a 3x3 matrix (Kernel) sliding over a 5x5 grid of pixels, where the central pixel's new value is the weighted sum of its neighbors.

sections.title: The 'Effect' of the Kernel (1:30)
sections.content: Show how different kernels act as 'feature extractors'. Explain that the numbers inside the kernel determine the transformation. If the kernel has balanced values, it smooths; if it has sharp gradients, it detects edges.
sections.example: A cat's whiskers: An 'edge-detection' kernel highlights the sharp lines of the whiskers against a blurry background, demonstrating how convolution helps computers 'see' structure.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Image Processing & AI (1:00)
sections.content: Connect the concept to modern technology. Explain how Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) stack these operations to recognize complex objects, moving from simple lines to complex features like faces or animals.
sections.example: A smartphone camera app: The app uses pre-defined convolution kernels to apply a 'Blur' or 'Sharpen' filter to your selfie in real-time.

sections.title: Conclusion & Summary (0:30)
sections.content: Recap the cycle: Input -> Sliding Kernel -> Weighted Sum -> Feature Map. Emphasize that convolution is the fundamental 'language' of modern computer vision.
sections.example: Analogy: Convolution is to digital images what a prism is to white light—it breaks complex inputs down into identifiable components.
